“Yes, burglar’s tools. That seems to ease your mind considerably. But what gave you such a fright? What did you think we’d discovered?”

Huck was cornered—the questioning gaze held him fast. He would have given anything for the makings of a believable answer, but none came. The gaze seemed to pierce deeper and deeper. An absurd reply occurred to him; there was no time to consider it, so he ventured it weakly:

“Sunday-school books, perhaps.”

Poor Huck was too troubled even to smile, but the old man roared with delighted laughter, shaking every part of his frame from head to toe. He finished by declaring that a laugh like that put money in a man’s pocket, since it did wonders toward reducing the doctor’s bill. Then he went on:

“Poor old fellow, you’re pale and worn out—you ain’t well at all. No wonder you’re a mite flighty and unsettled. But you’ll get over it. Rest and sleep will set you right, I hope.”

Huck was annoyed at having made such a fool of himself and shown such suspicious agitation. As soon as he had overheard the conversation at the widow’s stile, he had abandoned the notion that the parcel carried from the tavern contained the treasure. Yet he had only believed that it was not the treasure; he had not known it. Thus the mention of a captured bundle had overcome his composure. On balance, though, he was pleased that the little incident had occurred. He now knew beyond any doubt that this bundle was not the bundle, and his mind was wonderfully peaceful and comfortable. Indeed, everything now seemed to be moving in exactly the proper direction. The treasure must still lie in No. 2; the men would be caught and imprisoned that day; and that night he and Tom could take the gold without difficulty or fear of interference.

Breakfast had just ended when someone knocked at the door. Huck sprang toward a hiding-place, having no wish to be associated even distantly with the recent affair. The Welshman let in several ladies and gentlemen, including the Widow Douglas, and observed groups of townspeople ascending the hill to gaze at the stile. The news, then, had got about. He was obliged to relate the night’s events to his visitors. The widow spoke warmly of her gratitude for being saved.

“Don’t mention it, madam. There’s someone else you may owe more to than you do to me and my boys, but he won’t let me give his name. Without him we’d never have been there.”

It now showed that I was 132,000 feet, or twenty-five miles, above the earth. From that height I could see no less than one three-hundred-and-twentieth of the planet’s entire surface. By nine o’clock the land to the east had disappeared again, but first I noticed that the balloon was moving rapidly north-northwest. The curve of the ocean below was unmistakable, although drifting banks of cloud often blocked my view. I also noticed that even the thinnest clouds never rose more than ten miles above sea level.

“At half past nine I made an experiment, tossing a handful of feathers out through the valve. Instead of floating as I expected, they fell straight down together like a bullet, moving so fast that they vanished within seconds. At first I could not explain this remarkable sight. I could not believe that my upward speed had suddenly increased so enormously. Then I realized that the air had become far too thin to support even feathers. They really were dropping as quickly as they seemed, and their downward speed, combined with my own upward movement, had caused my surprise.

“By ten o’clock there was very little that needed my immediate attention. Everything was going smoothly. I believed the balloon was rising faster every moment, though I no longer had any way to measure how quickly its speed was increasing. I felt no pain or discomfort and was in better spirits than at any time since leaving Rotterdam. I kept busy checking my equipment and renewing the air inside the chamber. I decided to refresh the air regularly, every forty minutes, more to protect my health than because it truly needed changing so often. Meanwhile, I could not help imagining what lay ahead. My thoughts delighted in the wild, dreamlike regions of the moon. For once my imagination felt completely free, wandering wherever it pleased among the changing wonders of a shadowy, shifting land. First I saw ancient, venerable forests, jagged cliffs, and waterfalls thundering down into bottomless chasms. Then suddenly I entered places still and empty in the noonday light, where no breath of wind ever disturbed the silence. Vast meadows of poppies and slender, lilylike flowers stretched away into an exhausting distance, forever quiet and motionless.

“No, no, that’s tomorrow, and that’s exactly why I especially wanted to see Knightley today. What a horribly hot morning! I walked across the fields too”—he spoke as though he had been badly mistreated—“which made it much worse. And then to find him out! I assure you, I’m very displeased. He left no apology, no message for me. The housekeeper said she had no idea I was expected. Very strange! And nobody knew where he had gone. Perhaps to Hartfield, perhaps to Abbey Mill, perhaps into his woods. Miss Woodhouse, this is unlike our friend Knightley. Can you explain it?”

Emma enjoyed agreeing that it was very strange indeed and declaring that she could not say a word in his defense.

“I cannot imagine,” said Mrs. Elton, taking the insult to heart as a wife should, “I cannot imagine how he could do such a thing to you, of all people! You are the very last person anyone would expect him to forget. My dear Mr. E., surely he must have left you a message. Even Knightley couldn’t be that odd. His servants must have forgotten it. You can rely on that explanation. And it’s just what I would expect of the Donwell servants, who, as I have often noticed, are all extremely clumsy and careless. Nothing could persuade me to have someone like his Harry serving at our sideboard. And as for Mrs. Hodges, Wright has a very low opinion of her indeed. She promised Wright a recipe and never sent it.”

“I met William Larkins as I approached the house,” Mr. Elton continued. “He told me his master was out, but I didn’t believe him. William seemed rather annoyed. He said he didn’t know what had happened to his master lately, but he could hardly ever get a word with him. William’s business is no concern of mine, but it really is very important that I see Knightley today. Having taken this hot walk for nothing is therefore a very serious inconvenience.”

Emma decided the best thing she could do was go straight home. Most likely someone was waiting for her there at that very moment. By returning, she might save Mr. Knightley from giving Mr. Elton further reason for complaint, even if she could not help William Larkins.
